modules.title: First conversations
modules.summary: Greet people, thank them, and say who you are.

lessons.title: Hello & thank you
intro: Burmese is spoken with tones: each syllable's pitch, length and voice quality are part of the word. The coloured romanization shows the tone of every syllable (blue low, red high, purple creaky, green checked, grey weak).
Politeness is built into sentence endings. ပါ (bà) softens almost anything, and တယ် (dè) ends a plain statement. You'll hear both all the time.

lessons.title: How are you?
intro: Add လား (lá) to the end of a sentence and it becomes a yes/no question. နေကောင်း means 'to be well', so နေကောင်းလား is literally 'well?'.
Burmese usually drops 'I' and 'you' when it's obvious who you mean.

lessons.title: About me
intro: The polite word for 'I' depends on who's speaking: men say ကျွန်တော် (kyə-nàw), women say ကျွန်မ (kyə-ma̰). Set which one you use in Settings.
Word order is subject, object, verb: the verb always comes last. က (ga̰) after a place means 'from'.

lessons.title: Small talk
intro: A handful of reactions keeps a conversation going even when you understand very little: 'really?', 'good', 'nice to meet you'.

modules.title: The sounds of Burmese
modules.summary: Train your ear for the tones and sounds English doesn't have.

lessons.title: The four tones
intro: Burmese has four tones. They differ in pitch, but also in length and voice quality, so listen for all three.

Low (à): long and level, relaxed. High (á): long, starts high and often falls at the end. Creaky (a̰): short, with a tense, slightly creaky voice. Checked (aʔ): very short, cut off sharply by a catch in the throat.
In the script, ာ alone usually gives low tone, း (two dots) marks high tone, and a bare consonant or ့ (dot below) gives creaky.

lessons.title: Breathy consonants
intro: Burmese separates plain consonants from aspirated ones, said with a puff of air. English has both sounds but never uses the difference to change a word: the p in 'spin' is plain, the p in 'pin' is aspirated.
In romanization an h in front marks the puff: hk, hp, ht, hs.

lessons.title: Breathy nasals
intro: Burmese also has voiceless m, n, ng and l: breathe out through your nose before the sound. They're written hm, hn, hng, hl.
You've already met one: နှစ် (hniʔ) 'two'.

modules.title: When you're stuck
modules.summary: Phrases that rescue a conversation when you're lost.

lessons.title: I don't understand
intro: Negatives wrap the verb: မ (mə) before it and ဘူး (bú) at the end. နားလည် is 'understand', so နားမလည်ဘူး is 'don't understand'.
A verb followed by ပါ (bà) is a polite request: 'please do…'.

lessons.title: What's this called?
intro: Questions with a question word (what, where, how) end in လဲ (lé), not လား. ဘာ (bà) is 'what', ဘယ်လို (bè-lò) is 'how'.
Telling people you're learning usually earns patience and encouragement.

modules.title: Building sentences
modules.summary: A few patterns plus a few verbs let you say hundreds of things.

lessons.title: Everyday verbs
intro: Burmese verbs never change form: no 'go/goes/went'. Time and mood come from small words after the verb.
Learn these ten verbs as building blocks. The next lessons plug them into patterns.

lessons.title: Statements & negatives
intro: Verb + တယ် (dè) is a plain statement, present or past depending on context: သွားတယ် 'I go / I went'.
မ + verb + ဘူး is the negative: မသွားဘူး 'I'm not going / I didn't go'.
After a checked syllable (ending in ʔ), တယ် is said 'tè', without the d sound.

lessons.title: Future & questions
intro: Verb + မယ် (mè) talks about the future or an intention: သွားမယ် 'I'll go'.
Verb + မလား (mə-lá) asks a yes/no question about the future; a question word + verb + မလဲ (mə-lé) asks an open one.

lessons.title: Wanting & asking
intro: Verb + ချင်တယ် (jìn dè) means 'want to'. Verb + ပါ (bà) is a polite request.
ရှိတယ် (shḭ dè) means 'there is' or 'I have'.

modules.title: Food & family
modules.summary: Mealtime phrases and the people around the table.

lessons.title: Have you eaten?
intro: 'Have you eaten?' is a friendly everyday greeting, much like 'how are you?'.
Verb + ပြီးပြီ (pyí bì) means 'already done'.

lessons.title: Mum & dad
intro: အ (ə) at the start of many family words is a weak, unstressed syllable.

lessons.title: One to five
intro: Numbers are worth knowing early: prices, ages, times. Watch the tones: they're what separates similar-sounding numbers.

lessons.title: Six to ten
intro: ခုနစ် 'seven' is written with two syllables but said quickly as one and a half.

scriptModules.title: Consonants
scriptModules.summary: The alphabet, row by row, with the pattern that ties it together.

lessons.title: How the script works
intro: Burmese letters are built from circles and curves. It was traditionally written by scratching palm leaves, where straight lines would split the leaf. So look closely at where each circle opens, and what's added to it: a tail, a second loop, a gap.
Every consonant comes with a built-in short 'a' sound (creaky tone). On its own, မ is 'ma̰', not just 'm'. Vowels and tones are small marks added around it.
Each letter gets a memory hook: a word you already know from the course.

lessons.title: The sound grid: throat row
intro: Here's the big shortcut: most consonants sit in a grid. Each ROW is a place in your mouth (throat, palate, teeth, lips). The COLUMNS go: plain, breathy (with a puff of air), voiced, voiced (a rare spelling), and nasal.
Learn the pattern once and every row makes sense. This row is made in the throat: k, hk, g, (g), ng.
The rare 4th-column letters mostly appear in religious or Pali words, so we skip them for now.

lessons.title: Palate row
intro: Same pattern, further forward in the mouth: s, hs, z, ny.
Breathy partners again: စ (s) and ဆ (hs) differ only in the puff of air.

lessons.title: Teeth row
intro: Tongue on the teeth: t, ht, d, n.
တ (t) and ထ (ht) are partners: notice how often you've already seen both, in တယ် and ထမင်း.

lessons.title: Lips row
intro: Lips: p, hp, b, b, m. This row's two voiced letters are both used, and both say 'b'.
You now know the whole grid pattern.

lessons.title: The rest
intro: These sit outside the grid: y, y (spelled r), l, w, th, h, and the vowel carrier အ.
ရ is a classic trap: it's spelled 'r' but said 'y' in Yangon. You'll see it in ရေ (water).

scriptModules.title: Vowels & tones
scriptModules.summary: Marks around a letter set the vowel and the tone.

lessons.title: Long a & the high dots
intro: ာ after a consonant gives a long 'a' in low tone.
The two dots း always push a syllable to HIGH tone: the dots sit up high. Same letter, same vowel, different word: ကာ vs ကား (car).

lessons.title: i and u
intro: Marks above and below: a small circle on top is 'i', a hook below is 'u'.
The short versions (ိ ု) are creaky; the long versions (ီ ူ) are low; add း for high.

lessons.title: The vowel written first
intro: ေ is the famous trick of Burmese script: you WRITE it before the consonant, but SAY it after. ကေ is k + ei.
ဲ is 'e' as in 'bed', and it's high tone on its own. Add a dot below (့) and any syllable becomes creaky (squeezed).

lessons.title: Lego vowels
intro: Some vowels are two marks combined: ေ + ာ = 'aw', and ိ + ု = 'o'.
Then the same tone marks apply: း for high, ် to make 'aw' low.

scriptModules.title: Endings & stacks
scriptModules.summary: Final sounds, and letters that attach to others.

lessons.title: The killer mark
intro: The small mark ် on top 'kills' a letter's own vowel, so it becomes an ending.
Rule of thumb: a STOP letter at the end (က် တ် ပ် စ်) = a sharp cut-off (checked tone, ʔ). A NASAL letter at the end (င် န် မ်) = the vowel goes nasal.

lessons.title: Letters that attach
intro: Four marks hook onto a consonant to change it: ျ and ြ add a 'y' (in Yangon they sound the same), ွ adds a 'w', and ှ makes it breathy.
You've met them already: ကျေးဇူး, ဖြည်းဖြည်း, သွား, နှစ်.

lessons.title: Read real words
intro: Put it together: these are words from your speaking lessons. Sound them out letter by letter before you check.
